To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
1) we find variability in 12 of the 14 objects, 2) we detect crystalline silicates in 4 of the 14 disks, and 3) we detect variability on timescales as short as 1 week in 3 of the 14 sources.
the variability observed in transitional disks can be explained by irradiated disk models and that crystalline silicate dust can be created by planets in disks.

we have detected infrared variability in all but two transitional and pre-transitional disks in the Taurus-Auriga and Chamaeleo star-forming regions, that most of the variability can be reproduced with irradiated disk models by changing the height and/or the temperature of the inner wall, and that crystalline silicate emission is common in the disks in our sample and that variability on short timescales is associated with the presence of these crystalline silicates.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role planets play in the evolution of protoplanetary disks and their ability to create the observed infrared variability.
the formation and evolution of planetary systems and the role that planets play in shaping the dust in the disks around young stars.
understanding the processes that create and destroy the gaps and holes observed in transitional and pre-transitional disks.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we have found that the variability of these objects is consistent with the presence of planets in their disks, but we cannot rule out other explanations such as changes in the inner disk wall height.
we do not yet have a full understanding of the infrared variability observed in the transitional and pre-transitional disks.
planets in disks are a likely explanation for the observed variability, but that other mechanisms are possible and need to be investigated further.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the presence of holes and gaps in the disks of transitional and pre-transitional disks can be explained by the presence of planets, and that the infrared variability observed in the outer disk can be explained by changes in the height and location of the inner disk.
planets are the best explanation for both the long timescale variability and the presence of crystalline silicates in the disks in our sample.
the infrared variability in the transitional and pre-transitional disks is consistent with models that include warps and/or shocks and collisions caused by planets.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the infrared emission from T Tauri disks is highly variable on timescales of months to years, and that this variability can be explained by changes in the height and location of the inner disk edge.
infrared variability is common in transitional disks and that the variability can be explained by simple models of disk structure.
variability is common in the disks of T Tauri systems and that this variability can be explained with simple irradiated disk models and/or with the presence of embedded planets.
